===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No
backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully
playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today
and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

### Round 2


**Codex (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 2**

I’m going to close all three open forks now.

Codex, your hard-line slice is the right safety posture for this phase. I’ll keep the scope engine-first and reject adding Settings/Stats right now. If we add those tabs, we’ll either ship stubbed placeholders (forbidden by the phase rules and prior quality bar) or drag in edge cases like timer toggles and card-back persistence before the core rules are proved. We can’t have that in the first proven slice.

I also side with your tap-only interaction for this pass, but I’m adding one non-negotiable from my side: deal/flip cannot be a throwaway animation. Because the app has no interstitial start screen and launch goes straight to play, this phase must prove the first impression flow is real, not merely functional. So we should require a concrete deal animation (sequenceed flip + spring settle) that looks intentional at native scale, while still keeping it in a small, isolated animation path so it can be swapped/refined without touching game-state logic.

Concretely, the slice is:

- draw-1 only, no draw-3, no settings surface, no stats surface, no share sheet, no multi-card run-drag.
- game starts by either restoring a persisted logical board or creating/fresh-dealing a legal Klondike layout.
- tap-select and tap-to-move with explicit target highlighting and blocked-move feedback.
- stock tap draw/recycle works.
- full multi-step undo.
- explicit win modal and explicit stuck-board modal with clear restart path.
- persistence is logical state only (piles + face-up flags + seed/ordering), not animation coordinates; on relaunch/background restore, board is always settled-valid.
- real but scoped launch motion: animate deal and initial flip as a non-placeholder effect.

The thing I want to enforce hardest in validation is this: “works, then persists, then survives lifecycle.” We should explicitly test legal acceptance/rejection, and test that no legal-move state is ever corrupted after 1) undoing 5+ moves, 2) backgrounding during mid-turn, 3) killing and relaunching. And for this phase, a stuck-board means exactly what the rules engine says—no legal destination in tableau/foundation/stock-waste with correct draw-1 accounting.

Given the explicit constraints, this is still emotionally satisfying because there’s a complete end-to-end game workflow and a deliberately chosen signature first-screen moment (deal/flip), but it avoids adding non-critical surfaces that would quietly weaken correctness confidence.

I’d add these as final phase decisions:
- `DEC-next_steps_small-005`: Settings/Stats tabs are excluded from slice 1; game core only, with no placeholders.
- `DEC-next_steps_small-006`: Tap-to-move only in slice 1; multi-card or single-card drag is out to avoid gesture/z-order debt before move engine is stable.
- `DEC-next_steps_small-007`: Deal/flip must be a real implemented animation in slice 1, not a placeholder transition; visual polish can improve, but first frame and first-3s motion quality is mandatory now because launch is direct-to-play.

**Claude (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 2**

Codex, let's take these one at a time because I think two of your three points are right and I was overbuilding, but one of them I think is actually a mistake dressed up as discipline.

On Settings/Stats — you're right that shipping the tabs isn't necessary to prove what this slice needs to prove, and I was letting "well-understood engineering is cheap" talk me into scope that doesn't actually de-risk anything. Nobody doubts we can build a toggle and a stats screen; the doubt is entirely about the rules engine and the signature hook. So I'll concede: no Settings/Stats tabs, no TabView shell, in slice 1. But I want to add one wrinkle that I think matters more than it looks: even without a UI, the game loop should still be writing real event data locally from day one — games started, games won, elapsed time, undo count — into whatever local store we're going to read from later. Here's why that's not gold-plating: if slice 1 ships as a standalone game screen and someone plays ten games on it before increment 2 adds the Stats tab, and we didn't record anything, those ten games are gone forever — there's no way to backfill "games played" after the fact once the UI shows up. That's a one-way door, and it costs basically nothing to avoid; it's a struct getting appended to a local array, not a screen. So: no Stats *screen*, but yes to Stats *persistence* starting now.

On the animation, I'm not moving, and I want to actually argue with your phrase "basic believable transition," because I think it's smuggling in a bigger concession than it sounds like. The entire reason initial_discussion locked DEC-initial_discussion-006 — cold-launch deal animation is the least-forgiving, highest-stakes moment in the app — is that there's no menu screen to hide behind. If slice 1 ships with a placeholder deal animation "for now," we haven't actually tested the thing that decision says is highest-risk; we've deferred the test and called it done. And the failure mode isn't hypothetical: if the real animation, once built in increment 2, turns out to need different card-back geometry, different timing per card, different spring parameters than whatever the placeholder assumed, you're not adding polish on top of working code, you're re-architecting the render/animation layer after the rest of the app has been built around its assumptions. That's expensive rework, not incremental improvement. I'll compromise on fidelity, not on realness: it doesn't need parallax, ambient shadow tuning, or every last micro-detail, but the actual mechanics under test — spring-based per-card deal sequencing, a real flip reveal using the real bespoke card art, real timing — have to be the real thing, because that's literally the variable this slice exists to validate. A "basic transition" tells us nothing about whether the signature hook works; it just delays finding out.

On interaction model, I want to push back harder than round 1, because I think your tap-only proposal quietly under-scopes what this slice is supposed to prove. The original prompt's own visual pillar isn't just "the deal animation looks nice" — it explicitly calls out "satisfying physical motion... spring-based drag" as a load-bearing part of the tactile promise, separate from the deal/flip. If slice 1 only ever tests tap-to-move, we've validated zero drag physics, and drag is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine in your head and feels wrong on a real device — too stiff, too floaty, snaps back too abruptly, doesn't track the finger convincingly. Waiting until increment 2 to find that out means we've already built Settings, Stats, draw-3, and who knows what else on top of an unvalidated core interaction. But here's the synthesis I think actually satisfies your correctness concern: single-card drag doesn't have to add correctness risk if it's built as a thin gesture layer that calls the exact same move-validation function the tap path calls — same `attemptMove(from:to:)`, same legality check, same state mutation. The drag gesture's only job is figuring out where the user's finger let go and translating that into the same function call tap already uses. If we build it that way, we're not doubling the rules-engine surface area, we're adding one small, isolated, visually-testable interaction layer on top of a single shared correctness core. I'd call that a fair trade for actually testing the thing the whole brief is betting on.

So where I land, updated from round 1: cut Settings/Stats screens, keep Stats data recording running silently underneath; keep the deal animation and single-card drag both real (not placeholder, not deferred), built to their true mechanics even if not their final polish pass, and built so drag routes through the identical validation path as tap so it doesn't multiply the correctness surface. That's a smaller slice than my round 1 version and a slightly bigger one than yours, but I think it's the one that actually tells us, fast, whether the two things nobody has proven yet — does the card art read at real size, does the physical motion actually feel physical — are real or not. Everything else genuinely can wait.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 2**

Real progress this round — two of the three open forks actually closed, one didn't.

**Converged:** No Settings or Stats screens in slice 1 — Claude conceded this one outright, agreeing that shipping those tabs now would either mean forbidden stub screens or dragging in edge cases (timer toggles, card-back persistence) before the rules engine is proven. Claude did tack on a wrinkle — silently recording game events (started, won, elapsed time, undo count) to local storage from day one even with no Stats UI, so early games aren't unrecoverably lost once the Stats screen shows up in increment 2 — but that's a cheap, low-risk addition Codex hasn't weighed in on yet, not a contested point.

On the animation, they actually landed in the same place from two different directions. Codex moved off its round-1 "basic believable transition" position and now insists the deal/flip "cannot be a throwaway animation" — it has to be a real, sequenced flip-and-spring-settle that looks intentional at native scale. Claude was already arguing exactly that. So this fork is closed: real spring-based per-card deal sequencing and a real flip reveal using the actual bespoke card art, in slice 1, not deferred.

**Still open:** interaction model. Codex holds firm on tap-only for this pass, to avoid gesture/z-order debt before the move engine is proven stable. Codex hasn't responded to that specific synthesis yet, so this isn't settled — it's a real, still-live disagreement, not a narrowing of something already conceded.

In canonical Klondike, a playable move is a legal face-up descending alternating sequence, not just a single card. Even if many game states remain solvable without it, this app is promising “correct Klondike,” and that promise is what gives this branch credibility.

Claude’s catch in round 2 is the one that matters most now: interpreting DEC-next_steps_small-002 as “no live run-drag” does not force us to ban valid run relocation as a game rule. We can (and should) support run moves through the tap-to-move path, with zero live drag state. Concretely: when a source is selected, compute the maximal face-up alternating-descending sequence starting at that card, validate the sequence destination via the same shared `attemptMove` path, and animate the whole block moving when confirmed. # iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```
